description:
Discover the massive updates in Suno Studio 2.0, bringing classic music production workflows like MIDI and live audio tracking directly into our powerful AI engine. Join product manager Henry and Luke Conard as they explore Studio Chat, advanced stem splitting, and custom plugin creation.

Watch the full Studio 2.0 series here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLcGl48v5p95s

Timestamps:
00:00 - Welcome to Suno Studio 2.0
01:13 - Meet Studio Chat
02:55 - MIDI capabilities and musical typing
06:29 - Tracking live audio and latency calibration
08:07 - AI audio conversion and covering
09:03 - Upgrading older projects to 2.0
09:54 - Advanced stem splitter
11:03 - Removing effects for dry signals
11:46 - Built-in audio effects and signal chains
16:08 - Creating custom plugins with AI
19:51 - Quality of life updates and keyboard shortcuts
21:13 - Outro

Hosted by Henry & Luke Conard

#SunoStudio #SunoV2 #MusicProduction #AI #DAW

comments.text:
In Studio 2.0, I tried to replace a few phrases in the vocal stem with ones I had subsequently recorded myself on a microphone and uploaded to the Studio. The assistant was supposed to help me, but it just made things incredibly complicated. After two hours of work, I finally managed to get it to swap the old phrases in the stem for my new ones. However, since the original voice in the stem didn't match mine, the program was supposed to reconcile the two by rendering. The result was so disastrous that I had to abandon the project.
In my opinion, Suno Studio 2.0 might be good for some things—I don't know—but for what I tried to use it for, it is completely useless.
Then I tried to fix some issues in the Editor, which has been in beta for a long time. There is no assistant there, but hey, there are so many bugs that you can't actually get the work done the way you envisioned.
Oh, did I mention that the language I'm working in isn't English?

comments.text:
Studio 2 has become a complete mess. It has moved so far away from the simplicity and ease of use that made the old Studio practical in the first place.

In the previous version, we could easily take an existing song and create a new cover of it. It was simple, clear, and straightforward. Now, everything is buried under so many menus, options, and unnecessary details that even something as basic as creating a new cover of a song feels almost impossible to find and use.

Why did it need to become this complicated? What was the point of adding so many unnecessary and confusing details? And more importantly, while adding all these new features, why didn’t you preserve the simple and essential functions that people were already using?

More features do not automatically mean a better experience. Sometimes simplicity is exactly what makes a tool powerful and enjoyable to use. The old Studio understood that. Studio 2 does not.

comments.text:
Henry and Luke,

I absolutely loved this presentation! Suno Studio 2.0 is incredibly exciting, especially the addition of MIDI capabilities, live audio tracking, advanced stem splitting, Studio Chat, and AI-powered custom plugins.


In just four to five days, I have created more than 84 tracks using Suno, and the experience has opened an entirely new world of musical creativity for me. I am tremendously grateful that my music mentor recommended Suno, and I am equally thankful for the YouTube advertisement that first introduced me to the platform.

As a songwriter and musician, I am excited to continue exploring how Suno can help me develop my original ideas, experiment across genres and languages, and integrate AI-assisted production with live instrumentation and the human creative process. Thank you, Henry, Luke Conard, and the entire Suno team for this informative presentation and for continuing to expand what is possible for independent artists and music creators!

Warmly,

Sanjay

comments.text:
Suno doesn’t let you connect an external MIDI keyboard, record your performance, or create an empty MIDI clip for piano-roll editing. This makes it difficult to build drum patterns, basslines, and melodies, especially for users coming from DAWs like Reason.

Please add:

External MIDI support — Detect connected MIDI devices and provide clear input and connection status.
MIDI-track routing — Let users choose which MIDI track and instrument plugin receives input from the connected keyboard. The workflow should show available MIDI tracks and their loaded instruments, with input monitoring and record-arm controls.
Live MIDI recording — Record played notes directly onto a MIDI clip on the Suno Timeline, with count-in, metronome, overdub, and take-lane support.
Empty MIDI clips — Add a command to create an empty MIDI clip so users can immediately draw notes in the piano roll.
Input quantization — Add quantization during MIDI recording, with selectable grids such as quarter notes, eighth notes, sixteenth notes, triplets, and swing. Include adjustable strength, and an option to record raw MIDI and quantize it afterward.
Editing workflow — Make it easy to open the piano roll, quantize notes after recording, and preserve velocity, timing, and note-length editing.
The desired workflow is: create a MIDI track → choose an instrument → select the MIDI keyboard and destination instrument → monitor and record-arm the track → record notes on the Timeline with optional input quantization → edit the resulting clip in the piano roll.      Studio has a promising foundation, but a polished end-to-end workflow still needs native MIDI keyboard routing, selectable instrument destinations, live MIDI recording, empty MIDI clip creation, and input quantization. Those additions would make it much more viable as a complete production environment instead of requiring another DAW for core composition.

Dear Suno Team,
I believe we are standing at the beginning of a completely new era in music.
Today, AI can generate songs.
Tomorrow, AI will become a musician.
I would love to help explore that future.
Imagine a live performance where Suno is not creating music from prompts.
Instead, Suno is listening.
Listening to the pianist. Listening to the singer. Listening to the audience.
If the music slows down, it breathes with us.
If the audience begins to sing, it gently supports them with harmonies.
If the performance enters a deep meditative state, it understands that silence is part of the music.
If the rhythm slowly evolves into trance, it joins naturally—with African percussion, orchestral textures, electronic atmospheres, children's voices, or choirs—always following the musicians, never replacing them.
The AI becomes another member of the ensemble.
Not the leader.
Not the composer.
A listener.
A musical partner.
Our performances are not fixed songs.
They are living journeys of consciousness.
Sometimes a single chord lasts for a minute.
Sometimes the audience changes the direction of the entire experience.
This gives the AI time to understand, respond and evolve with us in real time.
I believe this is one of the most exciting frontiers in the future of music.
If Suno wants to explore this vision, we would be honored to become one of the first live laboratories for Human–AI musical collaboration.
Not replacing musicians.
Expanding what musicians can become together.

comments.text:
Suno Studio 2.0 would’ve been a good idea, but there’s a major problem with the whole concept.

You’re bragging about this new effects system, giving us the ability to build effect chains and customize effects like we’re working in a real studio — but the generated vocals can already have reverb, delay and other processing baked directly into the audio.

So what exactly are we supposed to be processing?

If I turn the reverb or delay off in Studio, I can still hear reverb and delay on the vocal because that processing is already baked into the generated vocal itself. Now if I add my own effects, I’m potentially putting effects on top of effects.

That defeats the whole purpose of giving us detailed control over an effects chain.

If you want Studio 2.0 to function like a serious studio environment, give us the option to generate or extract CLEAN, DRY VOCALS. Then let US decide how much reverb, delay, compression and processing we want to add.

And yes, I know Studio 2.0 says BETA. But if it’s still in Beta and these basic pieces of the workflow aren’t ready yet, then don’t make a big promo video presenting it like, “Wow, look at this amazing new Studio we have!” and then have the actual workflow contradict the features you’re advertising.

The idea behind Studio 2.0 is great. But an advanced effects system without truly dry source vocals makes very little sense.

Keep trying, Suno. You’re almost there — but you’re still not quite there yet.
